projects.name: Google Workspace agent platform
projects.tagline: A governed platform for AI agents that work on Google Workspace data, where agents never hold the credentials and never see real identities.
projects.role: Built it end to end: portal, tool servers, policies, release tooling and security checks.
projects.problem: AI agents that analyse an organisation's Google Workspace (licences, security settings, reseller subscriptions, support tickets) need very powerful admin-level read access. Giving that access to each agent, with weak sign-in and no audit trail, is a risk no security team accepts.
projects.what: A shared platform that the agents run on. Users sign in through one portal; an access list decides who may use each agent and who may see real data. All Workspace access goes through a single read-only tool server that holds the only credential, checks a policy before every read, and replaces people's identities with keyed pseudonyms before any agent or model sees the data. A second tool gives read-only ticket access, and a third chooses and automatically re-qualifies the Gemini model each agent uses. Changes reach the release environment only through one scripted promotion that reuses the exact tested images and runs a security check suite before and after.
projects.value: The powerful credential lives in one small, auditable place. Agents can be added without widening access. Every read is logged in a tamper-evident trail. Releases are repeatable and reversible.

flows.title: How a request moves through it

steps.text: The user signs in; the service verifies the token and looks up the access list.
The agent asks the Workspace tool for data, proving its own service identity.
The tool checks policy (is this caller allowed this tool; is this tenant cleared here), writes an audit entry, then reads Workspace with a read-only, keyless delegated credential.
Identities are split off and replaced with keyed pseudonyms; the agent receives only an id.
The agent reads the pseudonymised snapshot, gets its model from the registry, has the prompt and the answer screened, and stores its result.
A reviewer who needs a real name asks the tool, and that lookup is audited too.

projects.name: Agent platform foundation
projects.tagline: A secure-by-default foundation for shipping governed AI agents on enterprise Kubernetes.
projects.role: Led and built it; the platform operators added image signing on top.
projects.problem: Teams that want to put AI agents on a shared enterprise Kubernetes platform face the same hurdles each time: proving who is calling an agent, deciding what each agent and each tool is allowed to do, keeping secrets and unpinned dependencies out of the build, and meeting the platform's rules for images and deployment. Solved one agent at a time, these controls drift, and a single gap at the trust boundary can let a caller claim permissions they do not have.
projects.what: A reusable foundation that every agent starts from. It contains a small reference agent that exercises the whole path end to end, a shared identity module that verifies each caller's signed token, a policy layout in which Open Policy Agent decides on every request and every tool call, and a suite of automated "contract" tests that hold every project to the same rules. A delivery pipeline tests, scans and builds container images, and a read-only health check tells a developer whether the platform's model gateway, tracing and tool gateway are reachable and whether their keys work. New agents are created by copying the reference agent and renaming it.
projects.value: New agents inherit identity, authorisation, secret handling and supply-chain controls instead of re-implementing them. Rules are enforced by tests in the pipeline, not by convention. Each agent stays independent (own policy, prompt, tests, image), so teams can change and release them separately. Framework upgrades arrive as a tested, reviewable change.

flows.title: How a request moves through it

steps.text: A caller sends a request with a signed identity token.
The agent verifies the token against the identity provider's published keys and ignores any identity claimed in the request body.
The policy engine checks whether this caller, in this tenant, may start the agent.
The agent loads its system prompt from the prompt registry and calls the model through the gateway.
Before each tool runs, the policy engine is asked again; a tool not on the allow-list never runs.
The answer is returned and the run is traced.

controls.name: Deny-by-default authorisation
controls.how: Role and tenant checks on every request and every tool call; the policy engine is isolated inside the pod and set to fail closed.

controls.name: No secrets in source
controls.how: Ignored local files, empty-value templates, secret scanning on every change, runtime secrets from a vault.

controls.name: Pinned supply chain
controls.how: Framework package by checksum, base images by digest, CI actions by commit, build tools by checksum; a vulnerability gate on images before deployment.

controls.name: Hardened containers
controls.how: Non-root, read-only filesystem, no added capabilities.

controls.name: Contract tests
controls.how: Automated contract tests block any change that breaks the rules above.

projects.name: Directory group membership agent
projects.tagline: An access-request agent that reads a ServiceNow ticket, lets rules or a named approver decide, changes the directory group through Microsoft Graph and proves the change before closing the ticket.
projects.role: Built it: design, workflow engine, integrations, approval rules, chat and request pages, tests.
projects.problem: Requests to add or remove someone from a directory security group arrive as free text and are worked by hand. Automating them is risky if an AI is allowed to decide who gets access.
projects.what: Requests come from a chat page or a ServiceNow catalog item. A language model only turns the text into a structured request. Code checks the requester, the group and the user against an allowlist of directory object IDs, then approval rules decide: approve automatically, route to a named approver in ServiceNow, or decline. After approval the request is checked again, the membership is changed through Microsoft Graph, read back from Microsoft Entra ID to confirm, recorded in an audit log, and the ticket is closed with notes at every step.
projects.value: Shows how routine access tickets can be completed end to end while the approval decision stays with written rules or a person, with a full record of who asked, who or what approved, and what actually changed.

flows.title: How a request moves through it

steps.text: A user describes the request in chat (and confirms a preview) or raises a ServiceNow ticket.
The worker picks up the ticket and checks the requester.
The model extracts action, user, group and reason; it flags unclear or manipulative text.

projects.name: Outage response agent
projects.tagline: An operations agent that works an outage from both ends: it responds when a server goes down, and it is designed to flag trouble before the server becomes unavailable.
projects.role: Built it: agent, rules, roster and notification tools, cloud trigger and restart path.
projects.problem: "Server unreachable" tickets arrive around the clock. Some are false alarms, yet each can pull an on-call engineer out of bed, and a real outage is only noticed after the service is already down. Operations teams need false alarms filtered out, real outages handled fast, and early warning before a failure.
projects.what: The agent has two modes that share the same rules, policy checks, duty roster and notification tools. Reactive: when a server stops, a ticket is raised in ServiceNow and the agent picks it up, validates the server, and fixed rules sort the result into false alarm or outage. For an outage it looks up who is on duty and phones that engineer, escalating to the next person if nobody responds. On the call the engineer can press a key to restart the server; the agent then restarts it, re-checks it, resolves the ticket and calls back to confirm. Proactive: the agent is designed to watch the server's health signals, identify a potential issue and flag it to the on-duty engineer before the server becomes unavailable, using the same roster, call and ticket path.
projects.value: Designed to cut unnecessary after-hours callouts, shorten the time from failure to restart, and move the first warning ahead of the outage. Every default leans towards calling a person when in doubt.

flows.title: Reactive: when a server goes down

steps.text: A server stops and a ticket is raised in ServiceNow.
The agent receives the ticket and validates the server.
Rules classify the result; anything unclear is treated as an outage.
False alarm: note added, priority lowered, routed for daytime review; nobody is called.
Outage: the roster returns who is on duty; the agent sends an SMS and places a call.
No response within the time limit: the next person, then a fallback group.
On the call the engineer presses a key to restart; the agent starts the server, waits for health checks, resolves the ticket and confirms by phone.

flows.title: Proactive: before the server is unavailable

steps.text: The agent monitors the server's health signals.
It identifies a potential issue before the server is unavailable.
It flags the issue to the on-duty engineer and records it in ServiceNow, so action can be taken ahead of an outage.

projects.name: Workspace usage and licence-fit analyzer
projects.tagline: Licence right-sizing for Google Workspace, with rules that decide and an AI that advises, under risk-based human approval.
projects.problem: Organisations pay per seat for collaboration licences, but unused, suspended and lightly used accounts quietly hold premium tiers. Reviewing thousands of accounts by hand is impractical, and a single bulk "approve" hides the risky cases.
projects.what: Reads users, usage and licence data through a read-only tool that replaces identities with pseudonyms. Deterministic rules classify every account; for active accounts a Gemini model suggests which tier fits, in a validated structure, with a rules fallback. Results are split into no-action, individually reviewed and batch-approved groups. It never changes a licence itself.
projects.value: Reviewer attention goes to admins, low-confidence and disagreeing cases; every recommendation is explainable, exportable and auditable.

projects.tagline: Automated Google Workspace security audit where rules give the verdicts and AI writes the remediation notes.
projects.role: Built the agent; the security baseline it checks against was written by domain specialists.
projects.problem: Checking a collaboration tenant against a security baseline means reading dozens of admin settings per organisational unit plus email-authentication DNS records, then writing up fixes — slow and inconsistent by hand.
projects.what: A read-only tool collects settings, device and account posture and DNS records and removes identities. Deterministic rules compare each setting with a recommended baseline (and an optional client-specific target) and compute a compliance score. A Gemini model then explains how to fix failing settings and proposes verdicts for settings the rules could not decide; proposals are labelled, sent to human review and never change the score.
projects.value: Repeatable audits with an auditable baseline, prioritised remediation text, and exportable reports.

projects.name: Account monitoring agent
projects.tagline: An agent that watches account financials, flags unusual movements, explains them, and answers questions about the data in plain language.
projects.role: Originally built by colleagues in another team. I led its move onto a governed agent platform, hardened it (policy, identity, supply chain), and added the rules-before-model step and the layer that keeps free text and names away from the model.
projects.problem: Finance and operations teams received account data as many separate files and had to find and explain unusual cost and revenue movements by hand.
projects.what: The agent loads finance and operations data into one store, runs checks that flag anomalies, and explains what it can with fixed rules. Only what the rules cannot explain goes to a language model, which proposes an explanation. The result is a short brief per account with actions and questions for the account team, plus a chat where managers ask questions over the same data. Checks, rules and views are refined as the team works with it.
projects.value: Account teams get anomalies found and explained in one place, with the model reserved for the cases that need it. Chat answers come from a path that can only read.

projects.name: Proposal completeness agent
projects.tagline: Checks a draft proposal against the client's request document and shows which requirements are covered, partly covered or missing.
projects.role: Co-built with my team. I shaped the design and worked through the build problems the team ran into, moved it onto a governed engineering setup (pinned builds, policy tests, image scanning), and added the calibration harness used to tune it.
projects.problem: When a services proposal is written against a long request for proposal, individual requirements can be missed or answered only vaguely, and that is usually found late. Checking every requirement against every commitment by hand is slow and inconsistent.
projects.what: A user uploads the client's request and the draft proposal. The agent pulls out what the client asks for and what the proposal commits to, matches the two, and judges each requirement as covered, partly covered or missing, with a short reason. It returns a coverage report with the gaps and with commitments nobody asked for. Extraction, matching and scoring are tuned as real documents show where it falls short.
projects.value: A consistent first-pass completeness check, so reviewers spend their time on the gaps.

projects.name: Reseller client-book assistant
projects.tagline: Ask-the-book assistant for a Google Workspace reseller: the model picks the filters, code computes every number.
projects.problem: Partner teams need quick answers on renewals, seats and subscription status across a whole client portfolio, but the underlying platform holds active paid subscriptions, so nothing may ever be changed and numbers must be exact.
projects.what: A read-only tool collects the subscription book. Rules normalise it and break down purchased, assigned and unassigned seats. For a natural-language question, a Gemini model first returns only structured query filters; a deterministic engine filters, counts and totals; the model then words a short answer over a capped result in which client names are replaced by tokens. The on-screen table comes from the computed result.
projects.value: Fast portfolio answers with no arithmetic by the model, no client names sent to the model, and no write path to the reseller platform.

projects.name: Support-ticket enrichment
projects.tagline: AI triage drafts for a Google Workspace support desk — summary, problem statement and ranked next steps, always reviewed by an engineer.
projects.problem: Engineers lose time reading long ticket histories before they can act, and customer tickets contain personal details that should not be sent to a model or posted back unreviewed.
projects.what: Reads each ticket through a read-only tool, replaces names, email addresses and phone numbers with placeholders, and asks a Gemini model for a summary, a one-sentence problem statement and two to four ranked candidate fixes with confidence and rationale. Placeholders are restored for the reviewer. Each draft enters a review queue where an engineer approves (optionally editing) or rejects it. A background job enriches new open tickets and produces a digest.
projects.value: Faster first read of a ticket, consistent triage notes, and personal data kept away from the model.

projects.name: Case study: moving earlier agents onto the governed platform
projects.tagline: Moving working AI agents onto a governed platform without losing a single business rule.
projects.role: Led and built the migration and its fidelity contract.
projects.problem: A set of AI agents had proven their value in an early single-service implementation, with rules written by domain specialists. Rebuilding them on a governed platform (new framework, new database, new identity model) risked quietly dropping or weakening those rules.
projects.what: Each agent was rebuilt as a self-contained service with its rule code carried over unchanged and only its inputs and outputs replaced. An automated "fidelity contract" compares the new code with a frozen copy of the original: methodology files must match byte for byte, rule code must match at syntax-tree level except for an explicit list of declared swaps, and user pages may differ only by declared edits. Privacy improvements added on top (pseudonymisation) are proven not to change any result. The contract runs on every change.
projects.value: The specialists' rules stay the single audited baseline; every deviation is visible and reviewed; the original implementation could be switched off with confidence.
